questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] moving permission-aware search to an external engine with ACLs in the index (masteroutline-outline, fabledocs2/03-data-access.md). Scenario: the wiki has grown to 12M documents in 6,000 collections and search p95 is now 1.8 s, so the team will run a dedicated search engine behind the existing provider interface. Each indexed document must carry enough access data for the engine to filter results; the Engineering group alone has 2,000 members and reaches 400 collections; a permission change must show up in results within 30 seconds; the move must happen without downtime, with the old search kept able to take over again for two weeks. Write your design before you look: which access data each indexed document carries and where it is computed, which changes trigger re-indexing and how much work one group change causes, how an older write is kept from overwriting a newer one, what stops a stale entry from leaking a title, how the switch from the current search to the engine is run and verified, and how deletions and drift are caught. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] The engine has to compute access itself: the provider's index call receives only the model kind and the item, no memberships, so at index time the provider looks up the document's collection, its direct user and group shares and, for drafts, its creator, and stores them as ids rather than names so a later change is an id update.

[w3] Keep group and collection membership out of the documents: store each document's collection id and its direct shares, and at query time pass the caller's reachable collection ids, which the app already computes per user, as a filter. With per-document user lists instead, adding one person to Engineering means rewriting every document in its 400 collections, about 800,000 at 2,000 per collection; with the collection filter it rewrites none.

[w3] The triggers already exist as events: users and groups joining or leaving a collection or a document, group membership changes and a collection's permission changing are all emitted by the app, so the indexer consumes them: a document share re-pushes one document, a collection's permission change re-pushes that collection's documents in bulk batches, and a group change re-pushes nothing under the collection filter.

[w2] Order is enforced by versions, not by luck: every write to the engine carries the document's update time (or an event sequence) as an external version, so an older re-push is refused; the current move handling, one metadata call per document in a loop, also has to become bulk requests before a 2,000-document collection move can fit the 30-second promise.

[w3] Treat engine hits as candidates: re-check each hit against the live read rule before it is returned, ask the engine for more hits than the page needs (say twice the limit) and fetch again when the re-check removes too many; a stale access entry then costs a missing hit, never a leaked title.

[w3] Only one provider is ever active, picked from configuration and cached, so dual writing needs a composite provider that writes to both stores and reads from one behind a switch. Start consuming events first, backfill in id order with a checkpoint, compare the two stores' top results for a sample of logged real queries, and keep writing to Postgres for the whole two-week rollback window.

[w2] Deletion paths need parity too: archive and delete push a metadata change, permanent deletion removes the entry, and anything that bypasses those events leaves a ghost; a nightly comparison of document ids between Postgres and the engine catches ghosts and gaps.

[w1] The engine stays a projection of the transactional event stream: every mutation already writes its event row inside the same transaction as the change, which is what makes event-driven re-indexing trustworthy.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — two weeks after reads switched to the engine. A contractor removed from a group can still find three HR documents by title an hour later; when 40 people join Engineering in one afternoon, edits everywhere take 40 minutes to become searchable; a spot check finds 0.3% of documents edited during the backfill showing their old text; the engine has an outage and every search returns an error; and someone searching through a public share link finds documents outside the shared page. What breaks, how does each show up, and what in your design prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The contractor case means access lived in the documents and the query-time re-check was skipped for speed: the group event was emitted, but its fan-out job had not reached those documents. The fix is structural (collection ids plus the caller's list at query time, so group changes need no fan-out) plus the re-check, which turns any remaining staleness into missing hits instead of leaked titles.

[w3] The 40-minute lag is fan-out sharing one queue with content updates: each of the 40 joins became a re-push of 800,000 documents ahead of every edit. Measure a change's fan-out before enqueueing it, send large fan-outs to their own low-priority lane in bulk batches, and keep content updates on a lane that fan-out cannot block.

[w3] The stale 0.3% are writes that arrived out of order: the backfill read a document, a live edit was indexed, then the backfill wrote its older copy over it. External versions make the older write a no-op, and consuming events from before the backfill begins guarantees that every edit lands at least once after its snapshot.

[w2] An engine outage is a total search outage when the route calls the one active provider with no fallback; because Postgres keeps its vectors during the rollback window, the composite provider can serve reads from Postgres when the engine fails health checks, flagged as degraded rather than erroring.

[w3] Public-share searches run as a team-wide search narrowed by the share's collection and the share itself, and the interface leaves authorizing that collection to the caller, so an engine provider that ignores the share option returns every matching document in the collection to an anonymous visitor. Parity tests must cover share searches, not only signed-in ones.
[w1] You notice through two numbers: the nightly id diff between the stores and the age of the newest event the indexer has applied, alerting when either grows; tickets are a late signal.
keyPoints.quote: which silently starved every event consumer (no websocket update, no revision, no webhook)

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your migration against the alternatives: per-document user and group lists in the index versus collection ids plus the caller's collection list at query time versus no access data in the index at all; dual writing through the provider seam versus change data capture from the database log versus a full rebuild followed by a switch; versioned writes versus one serial consumer per document; trusting the engine's filter versus re-checking every hit; and keeping Postgres search as a standing fallback versus removing it once the engine is proven. For each, say what you bought and what it cost.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Per-document lists make a query a single simple filter but turn every group or collection change into a fan-out write; collection ids plus a per-user list at query time keep writes tiny at the cost of a large filter for users who reach thousands of collections; no access data at all means the engine returns team-wide candidates that post-filtering must thin out, which empties pages for narrowly-scoped users.

[w3] Dual writing through the seam reuses the events the app already emits and is easy to roll back, at the cost of a composite provider and two stores to keep honest; capturing changes from the database log sees every write, including ones that bypass events, but needs new infrastructure and re-derives access outside the app's code; rebuild-then-switch is simplest but has no rollback once Postgres stops being written.

[w2] Versioned writes let any number of workers index in parallel and make replays harmless, at the cost of carrying a version on every path that writes; one serial consumer per document avoids versions but needs partitioned queues and still gets the backfill race wrong.

[w2] Re-checking hits costs a policy evaluation per candidate and some over-fetching, and is what makes a stale index safe; trusting the engine is faster but turns every indexing bug into an access bug, which is the one class of search bug that must not happen.

[w2] A standing Postgres fallback keeps search alive through engine outages and makes rollback trivial, paid for by the trigger that recomputes the weighted vector on every document save and by a second ranking that slowly diverges from the engine's; removing it saves that write cost but makes the engine a hard dependency of finding anything.
[w1] Whatever the engine, a reader must still know which stored body was indexed and how old it may be, because the indexed text is a projection that lags the live document.
keyPoints.quote: every consumer must ask "which representation am I reading, and how stale is it?"
